label: Area-Preserving Diffeomorphisms
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 341 to 355 and treats two-dimensional symplectic dynamics as a concrete laboratory. Area preservation is the symplectic condition in dimension two, and the annulus twist map, the Poincare-Birkhoff theorem, and billiards each turn an abstract preservation law into a visible fixed-point or orbit phenomenon.

label: Area Is the Symplectic Form
notes: On a surface the symplectic form is just an area form, so a symplectomorphism is precisely an orientation- and area-preserving diffeomorphism. The defining condition is that the Jacobian determinant equals one everywhere, which keeps signed area unchanged and makes every later fixed-point count a genuinely symplectic statement rather than a topological accident.

label: The Annulus and Its Twist Map
notes: The closed annulus carries angle and radial coordinates with the standard area form. A twist map advances the angle by an amount depending monotonically on the radius, leaving the two boundary circles invariant. This is the cleanest model in which to watch how differential rotation across the annulus is forced to create fixed points.

label: The Twist Condition
notes: The monotone twist condition requires the angular advance to be strictly increasing in the radius, so the inner and outer boundaries rotate by different amounts. When these boundary rotations have opposite signs relative to a chosen lift, the angular displacement must vanish somewhere in between, which is the analytic seed of the fixed-point theorem.

label: Periodic Orbits
notes: A point is periodic of period q when iterating the map q times returns it to its start, and the orbit winds p times around the annulus. Twist maps support rich families of such p over q orbits, and locating them reduces to solving the displacement equation, linking dynamics directly to the calculus of variations.

label: Poincare-Birkhoff Theorem
notes: Poincare conjectured and Birkhoff proved that an area-preserving homeomorphism of the annulus satisfying the boundary twist condition has at least two distinct fixed points. Area preservation is essential: it forbids the map from pushing every point in one angular direction, forcing the displacement to change sign and produce crossings.

label: Why Two Fixed Points
notes: The displacement curve must cross zero, but a single transversal crossing would let a small area drift consistently, contradicting preservation. Conservation of signed area balances the region swept forward against the region swept back, which forces an even count of crossings and therefore at least two fixed points rather than one.

label: Billiards as Area-Preserving Maps
notes: A billiard trajectory in a convex table moves in straight chords and reflects so the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Encoding each bounce by its boundary position and incidence angle yields the billiard map on an annular phase space, and that map preserves a natural area form, making billiards a symplectic system.

label: The Generating Function
notes: The billiard map is exact symplectic with the chord length serving as its generating function. Stationarity of total length under variation of the boundary points reproduces the reflection law exactly, so periodic billiard trajectories are critical points of a length functional, tying the dynamics to the calculus of variations.

label: Periodic Billiard Trajectories
notes: Maximizing total chord length over closed inscribed polygons produces periodic billiard orbits, the simplest being the longest inscribed chord whose two-bounce path retraces itself along a diameter-like segment. Birkhoff used these variational and twist arguments to guarantee infinitely many periodic billiard trajectories in any smooth convex table.

label: Variational Viewpoint and Recap
notes: Across the chapter, fixed points and periodic orbits are critical points of an action or length functional, so the calculus of variations is the unifying engine. Area preservation forces the crossings, the twist condition organizes them by rotation number, and billiards realize the whole picture in an explicit convex table on pages 341 to 355.
